entries.title: Shenna Bellows Exits Senate Race in Maine
entries.summary: The Maine secretary of state’s withdrawal comes less than a week before Democrats hold a state convention to replace Graham Platner on the ballot.
entries.content:
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows dropped out of the race for U.S. Senate on Sunday, leaving three major candidates to face off at the Democrats’ state convention this week.

Bellows said she was withdrawing to focus on her role as the state’s chief election officer amid attacks on ballot integrity by President Donald Trump.

“Donald Trump’s attacks are only accelerating, and the best way that I can serve our state and country at this moment is by focusing exclusively on my role as Secretary of State,” Bellows wrote in a statement posted to X.

Trump addressed the nation on Thursday, arguing that recently declassified documents show rogue state actors are intent on disrupting U.S. elections and charging that hundreds of thousands of non-citizens were registered to vote, though evidence provided by the White House largely did not back up those assertions. Per the Constitution, state and local officials oversee elections.

The Justice Department sent a letter to all 50 states this month threatening to prosecute election officials if any noncitizens are found to have voted in any upcoming elections.

Bellows also pointed to the urgency for Democrats in this race, saying the party doesn’t “have a day to waste in unifying around” beating incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November.

Twelve Democrats, including Bellows, have entered the race to replace Platner, the party’s nominee who dropped out this month amid sexual assault allegations, which he denied.

A gathering of 500 delegates will join the 101 members of the state’s central committee to choose a nominee Saturday in Bangor, Maine.

With Bellows’ departure, the frontrunners are considered to be former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, former Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and former congressional staffer Jordan Wood.

Support for Jackson has surged among delegates after a televised debate last week, according to an analysis released Friday by Bangor Daily News. Among the 3,732 people who could fill those 500 delegate seats, Jackson carried 323 stated endorsements, Shah had 162 and Bellows had 48. The delegates were being chosen this weekend at county caucuses.

Jackson celebrated Bellows’ decision to leave the race, highlighting their “friendship” and “shared values.”

“Defeating Susan Collins will take all of us, and I’m grateful for your commitment to bringing Democrats together around that mission,” Jackson wrote Sunday on X. “Let’s get to work.”

Bellows did not immediately endorse any of the remaining Democratic contenders.

entries.title: Border Czar Says ICE Agents Will Wear Body Cams ‘Whenever Possible’
entries.summary: Tom Homan blamed Democrats for delaying funding for body cameras, an assertion Democrats dispute.
entries.content:
Immigration enforcement agents will have to record vehicle stops on at least one body-worn camera “whenever possible,” Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday, following two deadly shootings in Texas and Maine this month.

“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras,” Homan said Sunday ⁠on "Fox & Friends Weekend.” “I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action.”

Last week, Immigration and Customs Enforcement ordered agents to pause making vehicle stops during most enforcement actions, but quickly reversed course after President Donald Trump said Wednesday the agency wouldn’t stop one of its “most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”

The moves came after ICE agents shot and killed two people in separate traffic stops. An agent shot Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7. The Department of Homeland Security said Salgado Araujo “weaponized his vehicle,” a statement his family has disputed.

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian national, was shot and killed while in his car by an ICE agent in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13. DHS said in a statement that the agent who shot him was “fearing for public safety” but did not explain more.

Homan said Sunday that the rollout of body cameras for ICE agents was delayed because

Democrats blocked funding for immigration enforcement agencies during the 76-day partial government shutdown this year.

“Everybody in ICE would have a camera now if the government wasn't shut down by Democratic members of Congress,” Homan said. “There was money in that bill that they held up.”

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, disputed the contention that the shutdown played any role in outfitting agents with body cameras. A Republican tax and spending bill passed in 2025 included nearly $30 billion for ICE.

“This administration instead blew tax dollars on private jets and new souped-up, gold-coated SUVs that the agency cannot even use,” Murray told HuffPost in a statement last week. “The idea that Democrats are to blame for the Trump administration’s failure to deploy body cameras to the field and to protect people from out-of-control agents that they have failed to properly train is completely absurd.”

Then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced in February that the Trump administration planned to issue body cameras to all federal officers in Minneapolis following the deadly shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration officials.

“As funding is available, the body camera program will be expanded nationwide. We will rapidly acquire and deploy body cameras to DHS law enforcement across the country,” Noem wrote in an announcement posted to X at the time. That was before the lengthy partial government shutdown began.

In addition to the billions for ICE passed last year, Congress appropriated $20 million “for the procurement, deployment, and operations of body-worn cameras for agents and officers performing enforcement activities” April 30.

Only half of ICE field offices have the cameras, but all field offices are expected to get the new gear within 60 days, according to Axios.

entries.title: U.S. Service Member Dies in Iran Conflict, the Third This Weekend
entries.summary: Another service member remains missing, though the military says it found remains it is trying to identify.
entries.content:
U.S. Central Command announced the death of another U.S. service member on Sunday, just a day after an Iranian attack in Jordan claimed the lives of two members of the U.S. military engaged in the war with Iran.

A third service member involved in Saturday’s attack remains missing, though CENTCOM said “unidentified remains” have been found. “An examination process to verify the remains is ongoing,” CENTCOM announced on X.

The U.S. service member whose death was announced Sunday was killed in a separate incident.

“A U.S. service member in northern Iraq was killed in action July 18 during a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone,” CENTCOM said. Another service member is receiving medical treatment for a “minor injury” from that incident, CENTCOM said.

The identities of all service members who died or were injured this weekend have not been disclosed, the military command said, “out of respect for the families during the notification process.”

The latest fatalities bring the total to 17 service members killed since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. President Donald Trump has not publicly commented on the three deaths this weekend, though he told a NewsNation reporter over the phone Saturday that it was “a very sad thing.”

Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia), who is vice chair of the Select Committee on Intelligence, offered his condolences Sunday and denounced the conflict with Iran.

“This is what happens when you start a war of choice,” Warner told CBS’ “Face the Nation.” “I can say unequivocally there was no imminent threat from Iran.”

One of the Trump administration’s central goals in the war is to prevent Iran from retaining any enriched uranium for a nuclear weapon, but Warner estimated that it would take “15,000 troops on the ground” to secure the material.

“Nobody wants to do that,” he said.

The U.S. has launched nine consecutive nights of strikes on Iran, as negotiations for a peace deal and a ceasefire have crumbled. On Sunday, Trump called for Congress to pass additional sanctions on Iran in addition to those lawmakers are debating on Russia in memory of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.

“That’s what Lindsey wanted to do, and it was going to happen,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

This story has been updated to include CENTCOM announcing another round of attacks Sunday.

entries.title: Maine’s Troy Jackson Is on a Path to Become Senate Nominee
entries.summary: Two contenders, Nirav Shah and Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the Democratic race after Jackson picked up a majority of delegates.
entries.content:
Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson may have effectively clinched the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine.

Jackson, who is seeking to replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket after Platner dropped out, has the backing of more than half of the delegates who will attend next weekend's nominating convention, according to an analysis by the Bangor Daily News.

His position strengthened Sunday as two rivals, former state Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the contest.

On Saturday, 500 delegates and 101 members of the state’s central committee are scheduled to meet in Bangor, Maine. Those 500 delegates were being chosen this weekend. The Bangor Daily News reported that York County, which borders New Hampshire, put Jackson over the top, bringing his total of pledged delegates over 301.

“Thank you, York County. We’re organized, we’re ready, and we’re going to win. Solidarity forever,” Jackson wrote on X.

The delegates are formally unbound, meaning they are not legally required to vote for a specific candidate even if they promised to during the delegate selection process.

Shah said he would withdraw from the race to put the party’s energy into defeating Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November.

“Today I am stepping aside, and I am doing it for exactly the same reason that led me to get in: we must defeat Susan Collins, and the Democratic Party must be unified to do it,” Shah wrote in a statement posted to X.

Shah’s and Bellows’ exit leaves former congressional staffer Jordan Wood and 10 other candidates seeking the nomination.

The race to become the Democratic nominee for Senate reopened earlier this month after Platner withdrew amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied.

This story has been updated to include the withdrawal of Nirav Shah from the race.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
